cls: Aminomonosaccharide / symptomatic slow-acting drug for osteoarthritis (SYSADOA) - nutraceutical
pharm: Endogenous amino sugar and substrate for glycosaminoglycan and proteoglycan synthesis in cartilage; used as a symptomatic agent in osteoarthritis
quick: 1500 mg once daily (or in divided doses)
With food to reduce GI upset
summary: Glucosamine is a naturally occurring amino sugar used as a symptomatic slow-acting agent (SYSADOA) for osteoarthritis, most commonly as glucosamine sulfate 1500 mg daily. It is a substrate for glycosaminoglycan and proteoglycan synthesis and is proposed to support cartilage and reduce joint pain, though clinical evidence is mixed. It is sold as a dietary supplement or, in some countries, as a prescription medicine; it is not FDA-approved as a drug in the United States. It is generally well tolerated, with mild gastrointestinal effects, and caution is advised in shellfish allergy (for shellfish-derived products) and in diabetes.
indications: Symptomatic relief of mild to moderate osteoarthritis (especially knee)

dosage.d: 1500 mg once daily, or 500 mg three times daily
dosage.n: Effect, if any, develops over weeks

admin: Take with food to minimize stomach upset
Take consistently for several weeks before judging benefit
Use products labeled for source if you have a shellfish allergy
Reassess and consider stopping if no benefit after 2-3 months
moa: Provides a substrate (an amino sugar) for the synthesis of glycosaminoglycans and proteoglycans in articular cartilage and synovial fluid; it may also modestly inhibit catabolic and inflammatory mediators (e.g. IL-1-driven pathways) in cartilage, supporting a symptom-modifying effect in osteoarthritis.
preg: Avoid; there are insufficient safety data in pregnancy.
lact: Avoid; there are insufficient safety data during breastfeeding.
renal: No specific dose adjustment; data in significant renal impairment are limited, so use with caution.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment; data in significant hepatic impairment are limited, so use with caution.

moderate: Warfarin - case reports of increased INR and bleeding (especially glucosamine-chondroitin)
minor: Antidiabetic agents - possible effect on glucose control
Chemotherapy agents (e.g. etoposide, doxorubicin) - theoretical reduced efficacy
interactions.food: Take with food to reduce GI upset; some sulfate products contain potassium or sodium salts
interactions.diagnostics: May theoretically affect glucose and lipid measurements; monitor glucose in diabetics

counsel: Take with food and allow several weeks to assess benefit
Tell your doctor if you have a shellfish allergy, diabetes, or take warfarin
Stop if you develop a rash, swelling or breathing difficulty
Reassess with your clinician if there is no improvement after 2-3 months
This is a supplement/SYSADOA, not a substitute for prescribed osteoarthritis therapy
Choose a reputable product, as supplement quality varies
pk: Gradual; symptom benefit (if any) over 4-8 weeks
Below 25-30 C, dry place, away from light
pearls: Not FDA-approved as a drug; marketed as a dietary supplement in the US and a prescription SYSADOA in parts of Europe/Asia
Glucosamine sulfate 1500 mg/day is the most studied form; evidence for benefit is mixed
Caution in shellfish allergy (many products are shellfish-derived) and in diabetes
Possible interaction with warfarin (raised INR), especially in combination with chondroitin
Stop if no symptomatic benefit after 2-3 months
missed: Take the missed dose when remembered, or skip it if it is almost time for the next dose; do not double up. Consistent daily use matters more than a single dose.
overdose: Overdose is unlikely to be serious; large amounts may cause gastrointestinal upset. Management is supportive; there is no specific antidote.
refs: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements / NCCIH - Glucosamine and Chondroitin
